children: What is the Ozil goal AI trend?

The Ozil goal trend is a short AI clip of a night match where the person on the ball is almost never a footballer. Grandads in cardigans, office workers in suits, someone’s mum in a dressing gown: they all get the same few seconds of glory under the floodlights.

The beats repeat in every version. A goalkeeper throws himself into a full flying dive and misses, the ball pops up and drops onto the chest, a defender slides in and ends up on the grass, and the clip runs on towards goal. Creators call the move the “Ozil bounce”, which is where the name comes from.

The joke is the contrast: a scene that looks like a broadcast highlight, starring someone who looks like they wandered in from a family barbecue. That is why the outfit in your photo matters as much as your face.

children: Our generator needs no prompt: one photo in, a 15-second clip out. But if you want to try the Ozil goal scene in another image-to-video tool, the builder below writes a clean prompt for you. Pick a few options, copy, paste.

children: Original Ozil Goal reference sample, made from an AI-generated portrait.
Every choice rewrites the prompt live. The text stays plain English with no special characters, so it pastes cleanly into any tool. Nothing you type leaves your browser.
How to use the prompt in another tool
Pick one photo of one adult
who agreed to it. Face clear, good light, and ideally the whole outfit in view. Do not use footballers, celebrities or children.
and to the same length you chose in the builder. If the two disagree, the last beat is usually the one that gets cut, and the last beat is the payoff.
Paste the prompt and render the cheapest version first.
Short and low resolution is enough to see whether the face holds and whether the moves happen in order.
Change one thing at a time.
If the dive is missing, do not also change the camera and the outfit. One change per render tells you what actually helped.
Label it as AI when you post.
TikTok, Instagram and YouTube all have a setting for AI-generated content.
Why one-shot prompts often miss beats

The trend packs three distinct actions into a short clip: a goalkeeper diving flat through the air, a ball bouncing off the chest, and a defender sliding in and missing. Image-to-video models are generally best at one clear action per shot. Ask for three in a row and the usual result is that one of them happens well, one happens half-heartedly and one quietly disappears.
Timestamps help because they give the model an order, but they are a hint, not a schedule. Longer clips also give the face more time to drift away from your photo. That is why the builder has a
option: each beat becomes its own short prompt with the same person, outfit, setting and camera lines, so you can render them separately and join the best take of each in any editor.

Our generator uses MiniMax H3 with a fixed motion reference from the original trend sample, while your photo supplies the person. Results can vary. That is why it needs no prompt. If you want to compare the routes side by side, see the
What each part of the prompt does
If you edit the prompt by hand, this is what each block is for. Cut a line only if you know what you are giving up.
Tells the tool the frame and stops it inventing cuts or captions.
Keep face, hair, skin tone and body the same
Identity drift is the most common failure. Saying it up front helps.
Clothes from the photo, not a football kit
The joke is an ordinary person among players. Kit kills it.
Plain kits, no names, numbers or badges
Keeps real clubs and real players out of the frame.
Stadium, light, angle, full body visible
A side-on, full-body view is what makes the moves readable.
Dive, chest bounce, slide and finish
Times give the model an order to follow, even if it does not hit them exactly.
Crowd noise, no lyrics; a list of things to leave out
Cuts the usual extras: text, logos, watermarks, extra limbs.
AI video is unpredictable, so expect a few tries. These are general fixes that apply to most image-to-video tools.
Use a sharper, front-facing photo in even light. Shorten the clip, or switch to Three shots so each render is brief.
You end up in a football shirt
Pick an outfit preset or type a detail like "brown cardigan". Use a photo that shows the outfit clearly.
The keeper only slides on the grass
Render the dive as its own shot. Many models default to a slide because it is the more common move.
The ball never leaves the ground
Render beat two on its own and keep the camera side-on so the bounce is visible.
Text, logos or a scoreboard appear
Keep the Avoid line. If it persists, try the high and wide camera, which shows fewer boards close up.
The clip stops before the finish
Make sure the length set in the tool matches the length in the prompt.

The clip has one star. A group photo leaves it unclear who that is. Crop to one person before you upload.
